q: When a potential difference is set up between the two ends of a conductor, a ____ flows through it.
e: A potential difference provides the driving force that causes charges to flow as a current.

q: A steady current will flow through the conductor if a steady ____ is maintained between its ends by using batteries and generators.
e: A continuous potential difference is required to maintain a steady flow of charge.

q: Batteries and generators are called sources of ____.
e: These devices provide the energy per unit charge needed to drive current through a circuit.

q: The sources of electromotive force convert energy from some other forms into ____ form.
e: Sources of emf act as transducers, converting chemical, mechanical, or other energy into electrical energy.

q: For example, a battery converts ____ energy into electrical energy to provide electrical power.
e: Batteries rely on chemical reactions to generate an electromotive force.

q: In an electric generator, ____ energy is converted into electrical energy.
e: Generators use electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical rotation into electrical power.

q: A source of electromotive force has a positive terminal and a ____ terminal as shown in Figure 10.1.
e: Every DC source of emf has two distinct terminals with opposite polarities.

q: The positive charges are sent from the negative terminal to the ____ terminal within the source.
e: Inside the source, non-electrostatic forces move positive charges against the electric field to the higher potential terminal.

q: Alternately, it can be said that the main function of the source is to send negative charges from the positive terminal to the ____ terminal within the source.
e: Moving electrons to the negative terminal maintains the potential difference across the terminals.

q: Electromotive force, abbreviated as emf, is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the ____ circuit.
e: Emf represents the total energy per coulomb supplied to drive charge through both the external and internal circuit.

q: It is measured in unit of volt($V$), equivalent to joule per ____ of electric charge($JC^{-1}$)
e: One volt is defined as one joule of energy per coulomb of charge.

q: Despite its name, electromotive force is not actually a ____.
e: Emf is a measure of energy per unit charge (potential), not a mechanical push measured in newtons.

q: Generally, a source of electromotive force has an ____ resistance.
e: Real batteries and generators possess inherent resistance to current flow within their own materials.

q: The internal resistance of a battery depends on its size, chemical properties, life time, and ____.
e: Factors like temperature affect the mobility of ions and electrons inside the battery, altering its internal resistance.

q: This means that a resistor of resistance $r$ must be regarded as being connected in ____ to the battery.
e: Internal resistance acts in series with the external load, meaning the same current flows through both.

q: By Ohm's law, the potential difference across the resistor is $V=$____.
e: The voltage drop across the external load is the product of current and external resistance.

q: Similarly, the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one end to another of the internal resistance $r$ of the battery is ____.
e: This represents the 'lost volts' or energy dissipated as heat inside the battery per coulomb of charge.

q: The total work done in moving a unit positive charge round the complete circuit is $IR+Ir$, which is the ____ $E$ of the battery.
e: The total energy per unit charge supplied equals the sum of the external and internal voltage drops.

q: The equation $E=IR+Ir$ is called the ____ equation.
e: This fundamental equation relates the emf, current, external resistance, and internal resistance of a complete circuit.

q: Hence, the potential difference between the terminals of a battery when it is connected to an external circuit is given by $V=$____.
e: The terminal voltage equals the emf minus the voltage lost across the internal resistance.

q: When a battery having an internal resistance is used in an electric circuit, the potential difference between the terminals of the battery is always ____ than its emf.
e: Because some voltage is dropped internally ($Ir$), the available terminal voltage is always lower than the ideal emf.

q: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the ____ voltage (or available voltage) of the battery.
e: This is the actual voltage measured across the battery's physical terminals when current is flowing.

q: Hence, electromotive force (emf) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in an ____ circuit (when no current flows) as shown in Figure 10.3 (a).
e: With zero current, the internal voltage drop is zero, so terminal voltage perfectly equals the emf.

q: Terminal voltage(available voltage) is the potential difference between the two terminals of a battery or cell in a ____ circuit as shown in Figure 10.3 (b).
e: In a closed circuit, current flows, causing an internal voltage drop that reduces the terminal voltage.

q: Thus, emf is an open-circuit voltage and terminal voltage is a ____-circuit voltage.
e: This succinctly distinguishes the ideal maximum voltage (emf) from the practical operating voltage (terminal).

q: Charging a battery means the chemical energy of the battery which has been used up is now supplied back by ____ energy from some external source (battery charger) shown in Figure 10.4.
e: An external electrical source forces current backward through the battery to reverse its chemical reactions.

q: Therefore, in charging a battery, the potential difference between the terminals is equal to $E$ ____ $Ir$.
e: The charger must supply enough voltage to overcome the battery's emf plus the internal voltage drop.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when (i) discharging (in use) $V=E-Ir$, $V$____$E$.
e: During discharge, the internal voltage drop subtracts from the emf, making terminal voltage less than emf.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when (ii) open circuit(not in use) $V=$____.
e: With no current flowing, there is no internal drop, so terminal voltage exactly equals the emf.

q: The terminal voltage of a battery when (iii) charging $V=E+Ir$, $V$____$E$.
e: During charging, the applied voltage must exceed the emf to push current through the internal resistance.

q: When two or more electromotive sources (batteries) are connected in series, the resultant emf is the algebraic ____ of the individual emfs.
e: Series connections add the voltage contributions of each battery together.

q: In series aiding arrangement the currents leaving the batteries are in the ____ direction so that the resultant emf is $E_1+E_2$.
e: When connected positive-to-negative, the batteries assist each other, maximizing the total emf.

q: A connection of batteries where currents leave in the same direction is called series ____.
e: This configuration is used when a higher total voltage is required from multiple cells.

q: The total internal resistance of those two batteries in series is $(r_1$____$r_2)$.
e: Internal resistances in series simply add together, increasing the total internal resistance of the pack.

q: They can be regarded as a single battery having an emf $(E_1+E_2)$ and internal resistance $(r_1+r_2)$ in ____ aiding.
e: The entire series-aiding combination behaves mathematically like one larger battery.

q: In Figure 10.6 (a) two batteries are connected in series ____.
e: This occurs when batteries are connected positive-to-positive or negative-to-negative.

q: In series opposing, the emfs of the batteries are in ____.
e: The batteries push current in opposite directions, effectively fighting each other.

q: In series opposing, the resultant emf is the ____ between the individual emfs.
e: The larger emf subtracts the smaller emf, yielding a reduced net voltage.

q: If $E_1$ is greater than $E_2$, the resultant emf of those two batteries in series opposing is $(E_1$____$E_2)$.
e: The net driving force is the mathematical difference between the two opposing voltage sources.

q: In series opposing, their total internal resistance is still $(r_1$____$r_2)$.
e: Even though the emfs oppose, the physical resistances still add in series.

q: Two batteries having equal emfs and equal internal resistances can be connected in ____.
e: Parallel connections join all positive terminals together and all negative terminals together.

q: In parallel connection, it should be noticed that the same ____ terminals of the batteries are connected together.
e: Connecting identical polarities ensures the batteries do not short-circuit each other.

q: The resultant emf of the parallel-combination of identical batteries is just the emf $E$ of a ____ battery.
e: Parallel identical batteries do not increase the voltage; the output emf remains equal to one cell.

q: Since the internal resistances of identical batteries are in parallel, the resultant internal resistance is ____.
e: Placing identical internal resistances in parallel halves the total internal resistance.

q: This parallel combination can be regarded as a single battery having an emf $E$ and an internal resistance ____.
e: The lower internal resistance allows the parallel bank to deliver higher currents without excessive voltage drop.

q: In parallel connection of batteries, care must be taken that the terminal of the same ____ should be connected together.
e: Mismatched polarities in parallel will cause a massive short-circuit current between the batteries.

q: If terminals of opposite polarity are connected together in parallel, batteries may be ____.
e: The resulting high circulating current can overheat and destroy the cells.

q: Electrical energy is energy associated with the flow of ____ through any part of circuit.
e: Moving charges carry energy from the source to the load.

q: Electrical energy can be generated from source of emf such as batteries, generators, dynamos and ____ cells.
e: Photovoltaic cells convert light energy directly into electrical energy.

q: Electrical energy can be stored in other forms for future application using fuel cells, batteries, capacitors and ____.
e: Inductors store energy temporarily in the form of a magnetic field.

q: As the current $I$ flows through $R$, the potential at the point A is ____ than that at the point B.
e: Current flows from higher to lower potential through a passive resistor.

q: By the definition of potential difference, the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from A to B is ____.
e: Voltage is literally defined as the work done (or energy transferred) per unit charge.

q: Therefore, the work done $W$ in bringing the amount of charge $Q$ from A to B is $W=$____.
e: Total work is the product of the total charge moved and the potential difference.

q: The work done $W$ by the battery in taking the charge $Q$ from A to B is, in fact, the ____ energy supplied by the battery.
e: The work done by the electric field equals the electrical energy delivered to the component.

q: This electrical energy is transformed into ____ energy in the resistor $R$.
e: Resistors dissipate electrical energy as thermal energy due to electron collisions.

q: Heat energy is produced because the electrons ____ with the atoms in the resistor $R$ when they pass through it.
e: These collisions transfer kinetic energy from electrons to the atomic lattice, raising its temperature.

q: Since $V=IR$, the electrical energy $W$ produced by the battery can be written as $W=$____.
e: Substituting $Q=It$ into $W=QV$ yields the standard formula for electrical energy.

q: The electrical energy $W$ can also be written as $W=$____$Rt$.
e: Substituting $V=IR$ into $W=VIt$ gives the $I^2Rt$ formula, useful when current is known.

q: The electrical energy $W$ can also be written as $W=\frac{V^2}{R}$____.
e: Substituting $I=\frac{V}{R}$ into $W=VIt$ gives this formula, useful when voltage is fixed.

q: $1kWh$ is equivalent to $3.60 \times 10^6$ ____.
e: One kilowatt-hour equals 1000 watts multiplied by 3600 seconds, yielding 3.6 million joules.

q: Electrical power is the rate of transfer of ____ energy.
e: Power measures how fast electrical energy is being consumed or generated.

q: If the electrical energy $W$ is transferred in the time $t$, then the electrical power $P$ is $P=$____.
e: Power is defined as energy divided by the time interval over which it is transferred.

q: The unit of electrical power $P$ is the ____.
e: One watt represents one joule of energy transferred per second.

q: If 1 joule ($J$) of electrical energy is transferred in 1 second ($s$), the electrical power is 1 joule per ____.
e: This is the fundamental definition of the watt in terms of base SI units.

q: 1 joule per second is equivalent to 1 ____.
e: The unit $Js^{-1}$ is simply renamed the watt in honor of James Watt.

q: When electric current passes through a conductor, the electrons in the conductor are accelerated due to ____ field.
e: The potential difference creates an electric field that exerts a force on the free electrons.

q: The electrons collide with the other atoms and lose their kinetic energy which appears as ____ energy.
e: The kinetic energy gained from the field is randomized into thermal vibrations of the lattice.

q: The electrical energy $W$ supplied by the battery is transformed into heat energy $H$ in the ____ $R$.
e: The resistor is the specific component designed to impede current and generate heat.

q: The electrical energy $W$ is measured in joule and the amount of heat $H$ is measured in ____.
e: Historically, heat was measured in calories while work was measured in joules.

q: The relation between electrical energy and heat energy is $W=$____$H$.
e: $J$ acts as the conversion factor between mechanical/electrical work units and heat units.

q: In the equation $W=JH$, $J$ is a constant called Joule's mechanical equivalent of ____.
e: This constant defines how many joules of work are equivalent to one calorie of heat.

q: The value of Joule's mechanical equivalent of heat $J$ is ____ $Jcal^{-1}$.
e: It takes approximately 4.2 joules of energy to raise the temperature of 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius.

q: When $W=I^2Rt$ is substituted in $W=JH$, the equation for heat $H$ is $H=$____.
e: This formula calculates the heat generated in calories given the current, resistance, and time.

q: Joule's law states that the amount of heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to the ____ of the current.
e: Doubling the current will quadruple the amount of heat generated.

q: Joule's law states that heat is directly proportional to the value of ____ and the time taken.
e: Higher resistance causes more collisions per unit charge, increasing heat production for a given current.

q: In general, most of the electrical energy supplied to a resistor in an electric circuit is converted into ____.
e: Resistance inherently causes energy dissipation in the form of thermal energy.

q: The heating effect of electric current has special applications in ____ appliances.
e: Many household devices rely intentionally on resistive heating to function.

q: An electric light bulb is made of a glass bulb consisting a ____ filament.
e: Tungsten is used because it can glow white-hot without melting immediately.

q: The tungsten filament has a high melting point of approximately ____ $^\circ C$.
e: This extreme melting point allows the filament to reach temperatures necessary for bright illumination.

q: A small amount of ____, an inert gas, is added to the light bulb after the air is removed.
e: Argon prevents the hot tungsten filament from oxidizing and burning up.

q: The tungsten filament becomes hot when a ____ flows through it.
e: The flow of electrons encountering resistance generates the necessary heat.

q: At a temperature of $1800^\circ C$ the tungsten filament emits ____ light.
e: Incandescence at this high temperature produces a broad spectrum of visible white light.

q: Because the inert gas is added, the light bulb can be used safely up to the temperature ____ $^\circ C$.
e: The pressurized inert gas suppresses evaporation, allowing higher and safer operating temperatures.

q: The inert gas in the light bulb also reduces ____ of the filament.
e: Slowing evaporation extends the operational lifespan of the light bulb.

q: The electric light bulb converts most of the electrical energy into heat and ____ energy.
e: Incandescent bulbs are actually mostly heaters, converting a small fraction of energy into visible light.

q: In an electric iron, a ____ sheet is wound around the nichrome wire.
e: Mica acts as a structural and electrical barrier between the heating element and the metal casing.

q: Mica is a good electrical ____ and can withstand very high temperature.
e: It prevents the user from being shocked while enduring the intense heat of the nichrome wire.

q: When a current flows through the nichrome wire in an electric iron, it produces ____ energy.
e: Nichrome has high resistivity and does not oxidize easily, making it ideal for heating elements.

q: The heating element in an electric iron is controlled by a ____ that switches the current on and off.
e: A bimetallic strip thermostat breaks the circuit when the target temperature is reached.

q: The thermostat maintains the ____ temperature in an electric iron.
e: Users can adjust the thermostat to choose the appropriate heat level for different fabrics.

q: In an electric stove, a coil of nichrome wire is placed in the groove of the ____-resistant material.
e: The supporting material must endure continuous high temperatures without degrading or catching fire.

q: A fuse is a thin short wire of tin-____ alloy.
e: Tin-lead alloys have a low melting point, allowing them to melt quickly during a current surge.

q: A fuse is used in electric circuits to prevent electrical appliances from being damaged if ____ current flows through them.
e: Fuses act as sacrificial safety devices that fail before the wiring or appliances can overheat.

q: The fuse wire is fitted in a glass tube called a ____ or on a porcelain block.
e: The cartridge contains any arcing or hot metal fragments when the fuse wire melts.

q: When a current greater than the fuse rating flows in the circuit, the fuse becomes so hot that it will ____ and break the circuit.
e: Melting creates an open circuit, instantly stopping the dangerous flow of electrons.

q: When the fuse melts, the current stops flowing and the electrical appliance is not ____.
e: By interrupting the current, the fuse prevents catastrophic overheating and potential fires.

q: For an appliance rated as 700 W or less, a ____ A fuse should be fitted.
e: At 220V, a 700W appliance draws roughly 3.2A, making a 3A fuse appropriate for slightly lower wattages or standard protection.

q: For appliances above 700 W, a ____ A fuse should be fitted.
e: High-power appliances like heaters require a higher rated fuse to operate normally without blowing.

q: Electromotive force is the amount of energy provided by the battery per unit charge to move round the ____ circuit.
e: Emf accounts for the energy required to push charge through both the external and internal paths.

q: The potential difference across the terminals of a battery connected to an external circuit is called the ____ voltage.
e: This is the practical, measurable voltage available to the external load.

q: Electrical energy is energy associated with the flow of charge through any part of ____.
e: It represents the capacity to do work via the movement of electrons.

q: Electrical power is the rate of transfer of electrical ____.
e: Power dictates how quickly a device consumes or delivers electrical work.

q: Joule's law states that heat produced is directly proportional to the square of the current, the value of resistance and the ____ taken.
e: The longer the current flows, the more total heat energy accumulates in the resistor.

q: A fuse is a thin short wire of tin-lead alloy used to prevent appliances from damage if ____ current flows.
e: It is the primary safety mechanism against short circuits and overloads.
